content.text: Learn about the Voyager 1 space probe's history, construction, and components. Explore the various missions of the Voyager, such as its Jupiter and Saturn flyby. FAQ Will Voyager 1 leave the Milky Way? Scientists believe it is unlikely that Voyager 1 will ever gain enough velocity to leave the Milky Way. They also predict, however, that it may reach the Sun's closest neighboring star, Proxima Centauri, in about 16,700 to 20,300 years. How long does Voyager 1 have left? Scientists predict that Voyager 1 will be able to power at least one instrument until 2025. After 2036 however, Scientists predict the space probe will be too far out of range to send data back to Earth. Where is the Voyager 1 now? As of 2023, Voyager remains in interstellar space. Interstellar space is the area in the Solar System after the Sun stops having an effect and before the closest star to the Sun. Voyager 1 is a space probe that launched on September 5, 1977. The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) launched Voyager 1; its primary objective was to explore areas particularly far from Earth. NASA expected Voyager 1 to explore the outer solar system, the outer area of the Milky Way, in which the four giant planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, can be found. Voyager 1 was also expected to explore interstellar space. Interstellar space is an area out of reach of the Sun's influence that does not contain stars. The Voyager 1 was the first spacecraft to enter interstellar space. This image is the work of an artist that shows their impression of what Voyager entering interstellar space may have looked like. This program was to send four spacecraft into space to study the outer planets. However, due to the extensive budget that the mission would require, NASA replaced this proposal with the Voyager program. The construction of Voyager 1 began in the seventies and incorporated numerous technologies allowing the space probe to photograph and study the solar system. These technologies included an Imaging Science System (ISS), several spectrometers, and a Radio Science System (RSS). NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory completed the space probe's construction in 1977, and it was September 5 of the same year when Voyager 1 was launched. The technologies that NASA scientists included were expected to analyze and map the environments and surrounding atmospheres of the giant planets Jupiter and Saturn. These components include: To unlock this lesson you must be a Study.com member Create an account Voyager 1 was designed to explore the solar system's outer areas and interstellar space. Among its missions in the outer solar system, Voyager 1 was to photograph and study two giant planets, Jupiter and Saturn. The purpose of these missions was: Jupiter: Voyager 1 was to conduct a close flyby of the gas giant Jupiter, taking detailed measurements of the planet's atmosphere, magnetic field, and moons. The space probe flew by Jupiter in In March 1979. Saturn: Voyager 1 was to conduct a close flyby of Saturn, taking detailed measurements of the planet's atmosphere, magnetic field, Saturn's rings, and moons. This flyby took place In November 1980. Interstellar Travel: After completing its primary mission to study the outer planets, Voyager 1's mission was extended to include Voyager 1's Interstellar Mission (VIM). In August 2012, the spacecraft crossed into the interstellar medium, becoming the first human-made object to enter interstellar space. Voyager 1 still travels through interstellar space, sending back data about the conditions and environment found there. Since its launch, Voyager 1 has hit several significant milestones. Some other interesting facts about Voyager 1 include the following: To unlock this lesson you must be a Study.com member Create an account The Voyager 1 and its sister Voyager 2—which was sent to study Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune—have been significant to scientists and human understanding of the Milky Way solar system. More than four decades since its launch, Voyager 1 continues sending data back to Earth. For example, Low-Energy Charged Particle (LECP) instruments, which measures the properties of charged particles in the interstellar medium, and the Cosmic Ray Subsystem (CRS), which detects high-energy cosmic rays, continue to transmit information about the properties of interstellar space. Scientists predict that both Voyager spacecraft should be able to power at least one instrument until 2025, but after 2036 both probes will be out of range to continue sending data back to Earth. While scientists believe it is unlikely that the spacecraft will ever gain enough velocity to leave the Milky Way, they predict that Voyager 1 may reach the Sun's closest neighboring star, Proxima Centauri, in between 16,700 and 20,300 years. Currently, the significance of the Voyager mission remains its contributions to the understanding of the giant planets, its provisions of the first direct measurements of the properties of the interstellar medium, its work in capturing of the public's imagination and interest in space, and its inspiration to generations of scientists and space enthusiasts. To unlock this lesson you must be a Study.com member Create an account Voyager 1 is a space probe that NASA launched on September 5, 1977, to explore far regions of the solar system and beyond. Two regions in which Voyager 1 was expected to explore were the outer solar system—the area of the Milky Way in which Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune can be found—and interstellar space—the area beyond the reach of the Sun. The Voyager program was first conceptualized in the 1960s, after the Grand Tour program, a program requiring four spacecraft to study the giant planets, was canceled due to a significantly high budget. The construction of Voyager 1 began in the early 1970s and was completed in 1977. Voyager 1 consists of several technologies, including an Imaging Science System (ISS) and several different spectrometers, including an Ultraviolet Spectrometer (UVS) and Infrared Interferometer Spectrometer (IRIS). Voyager 1 had two primary missions. These missions included close flybys of Saturn and Jupiter to study the properties of their atmospheres, moons, gravitations, and rings and the study of interstellar space after exiting the heliosphere, a bubble-like area where the Sun's solar winds travel. Through these missions, Voyager 1 has made significant discoveries, including volcanic activity on Jupiter's Io moon, a ring around Jupiter, a seventh ring around Saturn, and previously unidentified moons surrounding both planets. In addition, aboard Voyager 1 is a record known as the Voyager Golden Record. This record contains images and sounds which are representative of life on Earth. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, which together comprise the Voyager mission, have significantly contributed to human understanding of the giant planets and interstellar space and have inspired interest in millions of people.
